title: Latency-sculpting harness and KV-churn diary
content:
Status: working draft / diary style. High-level goal: design a small, reproducible harness that can (1) create targeted pathological conditions for kernel selection and KV cache behavior, (2) produce a consistent regression signal for changes to scheduling/kernel heuristics, and (3) be fast enough to run in CI (nightly) and on-demand in lab clusters.

Summary (short):
- Problem: We occasionally observe regressions after kernel selector or scheduler changes that only show up for narrow arrival/token distributions or under specific KV churn patterns. Existing microbenches exercise throughput and simple latency but miss these modes.
- Proposal: "Latency-sculpting" harness — a workload generator + trace mutator that composes: interarrival distributions, token-length mixtures, KV access churn patterns, and prioritized route changes to sculpt the runtime into target states (e.g., high kernel-switch rate with moderate batching).

Design principles:
- Deterministic seeds and trace versioning: every synthetic workload is a seedable mutator applied to a named base trace.
- Small, repeatable experiments: single-run latency distribution must have <=5% run-to-run variance for stable traces.
- Signal surface: prefer latency percentiles (p50/p90/p99), kernel-switch frequency, KV cache hit-rate by prefix depth, per-GPU occupancy, and 'handoff events' count (router reassignments).
- Fast feedback: short runs (~5–10 minutes) that still produce p99 signals.

Harness components:
1) Trace Mutator (latency-sculptor):
   - Input: base trace (recorded or synthetic template).
   - Params: interarrival_dist (poisson|bimodal|bursty), mean_iat_ms, burst_ratio, length_mix (short/med/long tokens %), kv_churn_idx (0..1), prefix_reuse_profile (Zipfian parameter), route_shift_prob (0..1).
   - Output: workload file (ndjson of requests with timing and KV access hints).
   - Example invocation: 
     python trace_mutator.py --base traces/generic-1000.req --seed 421 --interarrival bimodal --mean-iat 6 --burst-ratio 0.25 --length-mix 0.6,0.3,0.1 --kv-churn 0.65 --route-shift 0.02 

2) Microbench runner (local/lab/ci modes):
   - Jobs: warmup (60s), measurement (300s), cooldown (30s).
   - Runs harness against a single runtime variant (kernel/scheduler commit) and collects detailed traces (server trace + batched kernel events).
   - Configs include measurement granularity (per-request tracing vs sampled every N requests).

3) Extractors & metrics:
   - Aggregates per-token latency, per-request latency, kernel-switch counts (a.k.a. kernel_transition_events), KV hit/miss by prefix depth, KV churn rate (unique prefixes per minute), and scheduler queue-length distribution.
   - Derived metric: Kernel-switch-per-1k-tokens normalized by batch-size (useful to detect regressing heuristics).

Key new concepts introduced here (should be captured in the harness and dashboards):
- KV Churn Index (KCI): fraction of requests in window W that touch a prefix not seen in last T seconds. Range 0..1. Higher KCI -> more cache invalidation pressure.
- Kernel Handoff Fraction (KHF): proportion of requests that triggered a change in kernel code path mid-generation (e.g., switching to a larger-seq-length kernel when autoregressive length extended). Measured per 1k tokens.
- Latency Sculpting Modes: "cache-erosion" (increase KCI quickly), "handoff-strobe" (rapid alternating token lengths to force kernel switches), "steady-long" (long tokens, low concurrency to stress memory).

KV-cache scenarios to include in the harness (priority order):
1) High-churn short prefixes (KCI > 0.7): simulate conversational workloads with many unique prefixes (customer support). Expected behaviour: KV hit-rate low, scheduler must avoid large batch accumulation; measure p99 token latency.
2) Stable prefix heavy (KCI < 0.1): ideal cache behavior; validate that batching and kernel selection give high throughput and low p50.
3) Prefix-population ramp: start stable then ramp KCI over 5 minutes to see transient effects and eviction policy interactions.
4) Hotspot + cold tail: Zipfian shape where top-1% prefixes are re-used heavily while long tail churns.

Scheduler stress patterns:
- Single large request walking through KV (long seq) coexisting with microbursts of short requests. Measure scheduler preemption/handoff count.
- Alternating priority lanes: insert high-priority short requests intermittently to force preemption. Verify SLA for priority lane remains under threshold without harming p99 of background beyond acceptable delta.

Acceptance/regression criteria (suggested baselines):
- Nightly baseline: run 3 seeds per mode; if median p99 increases by >=10% relative to previous 3-night baseline for any mode, open SRV-REG incident with attached traces.
- CI-gate: for scheduler/kernel PRs, run scaled-down harness (2 modes: handoff-strobe, cache-erosion) for 10m; block if KHF increases >25% or p99 tokens increases >15% vs PR-base.

Experiment log (selected entries):
- 2025-11-05: First prototype. Observed large variance in handoff counts. Root cause: non-deterministic sampling of kernel signals in the runtime's fast-path. Action: add deterministic sampling toggle (PR #246).
- 2025-12-12: Discovered a regression after kernel-selector change that increased KHF in handoff-strobe mode by 60% but throughput unaffected. This matched a live customer report (SRV-1428). Reverted selector heuristics and instrumented deeper counters.
- 2026-01-18: Added prefix_reuse_profile parameter (Zipf alpha). Found that for alpha>1.8 the scheduler would over-select large-seq kernels causing memory stalls. File: traces/alpha-high-20260118.seed.
- 2026-02-10: Implemented tight-run mode for CI (5m) but it missed a regression that appears only after eviction cycles (>8m). Updated nightly plan to include both tight-run (CI) and long-run (nightly 30m).

Preliminary numbers (lab cluster: g5x4-like, single model tflike-small, quantized profile qc-8):
- Handoff-strobe, seed=1001: p50=24ms, p95=94ms, p99=210ms, KCI=0.57, KHF=12.3/1k tokens.
- Cache-erosion, seed=1003: p50=31ms, p95=150ms, p99=420ms, KCI=0.82, KHF=3.6/1k tokens.
Notes: p99 sensitivity to KCI is stronger for smaller batch targets. We should log batch-size distributions alongside latencies.

Diagnostics we must capture (always):
- per-request timeline with kernel_id tags, kernel entry/exit timestamps, KV access deltas, scheduler queue snapshot at request arrival, host GPU utilization, and NVLINK stalls if present.
- a condensed "regression capsule" containing: baseline comparison CSV, two full server traces (candidate + baseline), and the trace_mutator seed+params that generated workload.

Deliverables and next steps:
- (Low effort) Add deterministic-sampling flag in runtime (PR in progress, #274).
- (Medium) Implement trace_mutator CLI and 6 canonical mode configs + upload to artifacts bucket. Owner: Marco. ETA: 2026-03-10.
- (Medium) Add KCI and KHF metrics into the console / nightly dashboards. Owner: Evelyn. ETA: 2026-03-24.
- (High) Integrate harness into PR gating with a lightweight runner (k8s job) that can spin up a single-node runtime with commit under test. Owner: Priya. ETA: 2026-04-07.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- How many modes are useful? Current set (3 KV modes x 3 sculpting patterns x 2 priority mixes) = 18 canonical combinations; running all nightly is expensive. Proposal: pick 6 for nightly (two per sculpting mode covering extreme/stable middle), rotate a larger matrix weekly.
- What is acceptable CI runtime overhead? We must balance signal quality with PR latency. Tight-run misses longer eviction-regressions: consider a fast pre-check (5m) then async full-run for high-impact PRs.
- Should we persist the generated workload seeds tied to every runtime commit so exact reproductions are trivial? Pros: reproducibility. Cons: storage and noise from long-tail seeds. Maybe keep a small curated archive of failing seeds + mode tag.

Quick TODOs (near-term):
- [ ] Marco: commit trace_mutator v0.1 with CLI and seed serialization.
- [ ] Jordan: add analysis notebook to /notebooks/latency-sculpting-explorations.ipynb (sketch attached inline below).
- [ ] Evelyn: dashboard wireframe for KCI/KHF and kernel-switch waterfall.
- [ ] Priya: prototype CI runner helm chart to run tight-run mode.

Notes-to-self / scratch ideas:
- Could use small RL policy to find adversarial seeds automatically (mutate trace params with gradient-free search to maximize KHF). Nice to have.
- Think about a short annotation format for traces so we can mark "customer-sim:small-chat" vs "bulk-inference:long-doc".

Appendix: example minimal workload snippet (ndjson style) — this is generated by trace_mutator as the input to the runner.
{ "seed": 1001, "mode": "handoff-strobe", "params": "iat=bimodal(4,20,0.2);lengths=(12:0.6,64:0.3,256:0.1);kv_churn=0.6" }

{"request":"<base64-input>...","arrival_ms":0,"prefix_key":"cust-312-ff","length":12}
{"request":"<base64-input>...","arrival_ms":6,"prefix_key":"cust-312-ff","length":12}
{"request":"<base64-input>...","arrival_ms":10,"prefix_key":"cust-555-az","length":256}
...

If you pull anything from this doc into an RFC or Confluence page, please preserve the experiment log entries verbatim (they help correlate infra changes with signals).

End of diary entry. Feedback welcome — tagging team leads in the linked slack thread to schedule a short sync (30m) to align on what goes into CI vs nightly.
